claims.text: Sudden, ongoing attack: pulse oximetry, fingerstick glucose, a pregnancy test in females, and usually an ECG.
claims.quote: Patients with a sudden, ongoing attack should have pulse oximetry and fingerstick glucose test. Female patients should have a pregnancy test. Most clinicians also do electrocardiography (ECG).

claims.text: Acute symptoms with headache, neurologic abnormalities or other central signs: generally gadolinium-enhanced MRI.
claims.quote: generally gadolinium-enhanced magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is indicated for patients with acute symptoms who have headache, neurologic abnormalities, or any other findings suggestive of a central nervous system etiology.

claims.text: Chronic central vestibular symptoms: gadolinium-enhanced MRI for stroke, multiple sclerosis or other CNS lesions.
claims.quote: Patients with chronic symptoms of central vestibular pathology should have gadolinium-enhanced MRI to look for evidence of stroke, multiple sclerosis, or other central nervous system lesions.

claims.text: Abnormal or equivocal bedside hearing and vestibular tests: formal audiometry and electronystagmography.
claims.quote: Patients for whom results of bedside tests of hearing and vestibular function are abnormal or equivocal should undergo formal testing with audiometry and electronystagmography.

claims.text: Heart: ECG, Holter monitoring, echocardiography and exercise stress testing as needed.
claims.quote: ECG, Holter monitoring for heart rhythm abnormalities, echocardiography, and exercise stress testing may be done to evaluate heart function.

claims.text: Labs rarely help, except syphilis serology for chronic vertigo with bilateral hearing loss.
claims.quote: Laboratory tests are rarely helpful, except for patients with chronic vertigo and bilateral hearing loss, for whom syphilis serology is indicated.
